question: Does the published evidence support nudges as an effective policy tool after correcting for publication bias?

coverage.note: Have Mertens 2022 raw pooled effect size context and DellaVigna/Linos citation, but missing actual raw effect size numbers (e.g. Cohen's d value) and explicit list of bias-correction methods applied per meta-analysis (p-curve, PET-PEESE, trim-and-fill results specifically for Mertens).
No concrete pre/post-correction effect size numbers or significance comparisons (e.g. d=0.4 raw vs d=0.08 corrected) have been extracted yet.
DellaVigna & Linos 126 RCTs and a related 124-RCT dataset are referenced as comparison points, but no direct numeric comparison (academic vs government effect sizes) has been captured.

COVID vaccine nudge subgroup data (social norms vs defaults vs reminders) shows variation, but this is domain-specific (vaccination) and not tied to publication-bias correction; broader nudge-category bias-correction breakdown from Mertens is missing.

Good methodological critique of PET-PEESE reliability under heterogeneity is captured, but no direct comparison of convergence/divergence across p-curve vs PET-PEESE vs trim-and-fill applied to the same nudge dataset.
No evidence gathered yet on cost-effectiveness of nudges relative to other policy tools post-correction.
COVID vaccine nudge meta-analysis (2022/2023) shows weakening effects over time, but no broader post-2020 pre-registered multi-site replication evidence outside health/vaccine domain.

COVID nudge effect weakening over time and 'small magnitude' conclusion offers a partial counter-example, but no high-powered null-result flagship study (e.g. behavioral science mega-studies) has been identified.

contradictions: The Vlaev et al. 2016 review concluded nudges are 'powerful policy tools for influencing health behavior' based on pre-2020 published literature, but this specific pro-nudge conclusion claim was explicitly killed by the adversarial panel (support+provenance issues) and cannot be used as evidence; meanwhile post-2020 bias-correction work (Maier et al. 2022) directly challenges the pre-correction literature this review relied on.

Two peer-reviewed methodological sources disagree on the reliability of PET-PEESE-family corrections under realistic conditions: doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1298 states FPP 'becomes unreliable' under heterogeneity (the realistic case for literatures like nudge research), while doi.org/10.1177/1948550617693062 (Stanley/Doucouliagos lineage) claims PET-PEESE has statistical properties 'much better than conventional meta-analysis' even under adverse conditions.

The Vlaev et al. 2016 Public Administration Review piece concludes nudges are 'powerful policy tools' based on pre-2020 published literature, while later bias-correction work (Mertens 2022 critique, PET-PEESE reliability studies) implies raw published effects are likely inflated and unreliable under heterogeneity — these framings are in tension though not a direct empirical contradiction yet, since no corrected effect size number has been extracted to confirm the discrepancy.

Stanley & Doucouliagos-related source (doi.org/10.1177/1948550617693062) claims PET-PEESE has statistical properties 'much better than conventional meta-analysis' even under adverse conditions, while doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1298 claims FAT-PET-PEESE 'becomes unreliable' for heterogeneous data (the realistic case for nudge research) — these two secondary/primary sources offer conflicting reliability assessments of the same correction method under similar problematic conditions (small samples, heterogeneity).

scopeContract.decisionAtStake: Whether a policymaker, funder, or research team should continue treating nudges as a reliably effective, low-cost policy lever worth prioritizing/scaling (vs. treating published nudge effect sizes as inflated and either downgrading expected impact, demanding larger pre-registered trials before scaling, or shifting resources toward alternative interventions like mandates/incentives).
scopeContract.keyQuestion: After applying publication-bias correction methods to the nudge literature, do corrected/bias-adjusted average effect sizes remain large and consistent enough (e.g., comparable to those found in large unpublished/pre-registered government trials) to justify nudges as an effective standalone policy tool, or do they shrink toward null/trivial?
assumptions: Scope covers behavioral/nudge interventions as popularized post-Thaler & Sunstein (2008), primarily in public policy contexts (health, savings, energy, tax compliance) rather than pure marketing/private-sector nudges.
Geography: evidence base is predominantly US/UK/EU/Australia government and academic trials; findings may not generalize to low-income countries or non-WEIRD populations.

Time horizon: literature through ~2023-2024, including the major meta-analyses and bias-correction papers (e.g., DellaVigna & Linos 2022; Mertens et al. 2022; Maier et al. 2022) that triggered the 'nudge replication crisis' debate.

'Effective' is interpreted as producing statistically and practically meaningful behavior change (not just p<0.05) relative to a plausible counterfactual policy (e.g., regulation, incentives, defaults vs. no intervention).

'Corrected for publication bias' means applying formal methods (p-curve, trim-and-fill, PET-PEER, funnel plot asymmetry tests, or comparing registered/pre-registered large-scale field trials vs. published lab/small studies) rather than just noting bias exists qualitatively.
Currency/units: effect sizes assumed reported in percentage-point behavior change or standardized mean differences as commonly used in this literature.
Excludes COVID-specific nudge studies unless part of broader meta-analytic samples, since that literature has its own idiosyncratic conditions.
whatWouldChangeTheAnswer: If bias-correction techniques (p-curve, PET-PEER, funnel asymmetry) applied to major meta-analyses show corrected effect sizes shrink by >50% but remain statistically/practically significant → supports 'modest but real' verdict.

If large-scale registered field trials/government mega-studies (e.g., DellaVigna & Linos analysis of 126 RCTs run by US/UK nudge units) show effects roughly an order of magnitude smaller than published academic literature → strongly supports 'inflated, not effective at scale' verdict.

If corrected effects vary drastically by nudge type (e.g., defaults remain robust while social-norm messaging collapses to null) → flips answer from a single verdict to a conditional, type-dependent verdict.

If evidence shows publication bias is minimal or bias-correction methods themselves are contested/unreliable for this literature → supports 'evidence remains credible' verdict, undermining the premise of the question.

If newer pre-registered replications and multi-site trials (post-2020) show effects converging with corrected meta-analytic estimates rather than diverging → supports credibility of nudges despite historical bias.
Discovery that bias correction primarily affects lab/survey-based nudge studies but not field RCTs (or vice versa) would change which subset of 'nudge evidence' the conclusion applies to.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Nudges remain an effective policy tool: bias-corrected effect sizes, while smaller than raw published estimates, are still meaningfully positive and comparable across independent large-scale/registered trials.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding that bias-corrected meta-analytic estimates (e.g., via p-curve/PET-PEER) are statistically indistinguishable from zero, OR that large pre-registered government mega-studies show near-zero average effects.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Nudges are substantially overstated: publication bias inflated effect sizes considerably (e.g., 2-8x), and corrected effects, though nonzero, are too small to justify nudges as a primary/standalone policy tool (better as a low-cost complement, not a substitute for stronger interventions).
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding that corrected effects remain large (e.g., within ~20-30% of original published estimates) and consistent with unpublished/registered trial results, showing publication bias was not a major driver of the literature's headline claims.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Effectiveness is heterogeneous/type-dependent: some nudge categories (e.g., defaults, active choice) survive bias correction with real effects, while others (e.g., social norms, simplification messaging) shrink to near-null, making a single yes/no verdict inappropriate.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding that bias-correction effects are roughly uniform across nudge types (all shrink similarly or all remain robust similarly), removing the basis for a differentiated verdict.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The publication-bias-correction methods themselves are too unreliable/contested in this literature (due to heterogeneity, non-independence of effects, or p-curve misapplication) to draw a confident corrected estimate either way, making the question currently unanswerable with high confidence.
hypotheses.killCriterion: Finding strong methodological consensus (multiple independent bias-correction approaches converging on similar corrected estimates) that resolves the direction and magnitude of publication bias impact.

summary: The confirmed evidence documents that a major pro-nudge meta-analysis (Mertens et al. 2022, PNAS, 455 effect sizes/214 studies/N=2.1M) exists and was directly challenged by a bias-correction rebuttal (Maier et al. 2022, PNAS), but the actual bias-corrected effect-size numbers from that rebuttal were never captured or audited in this evidence set, so no direct quantitative before/after comparison can be reported. Independently, peer-reviewed methodological sources show that the standard bias-correction technique underlying such rebuttals (FAT-PET-PEESE/PET-PEESE) is reliable only under an unrealistic fixed-effects assumption and becomes unreliable - for detecting bias, for hypothesis-testing, and less efficient for mean-effect estimation - precisely under the heterogeneous, small-sample conditions typical of behavioral literatures like nudge research, and these methodological sources themselves disagree on how much to trust the correction under adverse conditions. Domain-specific evidence in COVID-19 vaccination nudges shows real but modest, significant pooled effects (RR 1.19), alongside qualitative acknowledgment across the broader literature of "growing concern" about efficacy and "mixed" empirical results for digital nudging. Given the missing hinge number and the documented unreliability/contestation of the correction methods themselves, the evidence supports H4 (methodological unreliability precludes a confident corrected verdict) rather than a clean yes (H1) or no (H2) answer.
answerFirst: The published evidence does NOT allow a confident "yes, nudges remain effective after bias correction" — nor does it allow a confident "no." The gathered claims establish that (a) the flagship pro-nudge meta-analysis (Mertens et al. 2022, PNAS) exists and was directly challenged by Maier et al. (2022, PNAS) using publication-bias-correction methods, but (b) the specific bias-corrected effect-size numbers, and the pre/post-correction magnitude comparison, were never captured in the confirmed evidence set, and (c) the correction method itself (FAT-PET-PEESE/PET-PEESE) is shown by methodological sources to be unreliable precisely in the heterogeneous, small-sample, high-variance conditions that characterize the nudge literature. The most defensible verdict is H4 (the correction methods are too contested/unreliable in this literature to yield a high-confidence corrected estimate), with H1–H3 untested for lack of a captured hinge number.

hingeNumber.value: Not established - no confirmed claim reports Maier et al.'s (2022) actual bias-corrected pooled effect size or its confidence interval relative to zero.
hingeNumber.why: The entire question (does nudging remain effective after bias correction) hinges on comparing Mertens et al.'s raw pooled effect size to Maier et al.'s bias-corrected estimate; without both numbers side by side, no magnitude-of-shrinkage or distinguishability-from-zero judgment can be made.
hingeNumber.sensitivity: Because this number was never captured, the overall verdict cannot be sensitivity-tested; any assumed value would be fabrication. This absence is itself the reason the call must be H4 (unresolved) rather than H1 or H2.
hingeNumber.source: Missing - flagged as unanswered in the coverage checklist ('By what magnitude do bias-corrected effect sizes shrink relative to raw published estimates...')

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H1: Nudges remain an effective policy tool - bias-corrected effect sizes, while smaller than raw estimates, remain meaningfully positive and comparable across independent large-scale/registered trials.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: No confirmed claim reports an actual bias-corrected effect-size estimate (from Maier et al. or otherwise) with a magnitude and CI that could be judged 'meaningfully positive.' The COVID-vaccine domain findings (claims [7], [19]) show small-but-significant raw pooled effects, but these are not publication-bias-corrected estimates of the general nudge literature, so they cannot confirm or kill H1.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H2: Nudges are substantially overstated - publication bias inflated effects considerably, and corrected effects, though nonzero, are too small to be a primary policy tool.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: The existence of the Maier et al. (2022) rebuttal titled 'No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias' (claim [3]) is suggestive but was only audited via a secondary citation, not the primary paper's actual numeric results. No confirmed claim quantifies the shrinkage magnitude (e.g., 2-8x) needed to positively confirm H2, nor does any claim show corrected effects remaining large enough to kill H2. Genuinely untested pending the missing hinge number.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H3: Effectiveness is heterogeneous/type-dependent - some nudge categories survive correction, others do not.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: The only nudge-type subgroup breakdown that was gathered (social norms vs. defaults vs. reminders effect sizes) was explicitly refuted/killed by the adversarial panel and cannot be cited as evidence. No surviving confirmed claim compares bias-corrected effects across nudge categories.

hypothesisVerdicts.hypothesis: H4: The publication-bias-correction methods themselves are too unreliable/contested in this literature to draw a confident corrected estimate either way, making the question currently unanswerable with high confidence.
hypothesisVerdicts.reasoning: Multiple peer-reviewed methodological sources directly support this: FAT-PET-PEESE performs well only under an unrealistic fixed-effects assumption and becomes unreliable for bias-testing and hypothesis-testing under heterogeneity (claim [0], [8], [22]); PET-PEESE separately is shown to perform poorly with few studies, small samples, and high heterogeneity (claim [18]) - conditions plausible for the nudge literature. Additionally, the methodological sources themselves disagree with each other on how reliable PET-PEESE is under adverse conditions (flagged contradiction), which is direct evidence of contested methodological consensus rather than convergence. This does not 'kill' H4's kill-criterion (which required strong convergence across methods) - instead the evidence affirmatively supports persistent contestation, so H4 survives.

strongestArgumentAgainst: The strongest case against concluding "insufficient evidence" is that the mere existence of a dedicated, PNAS-published rebuttal paper titled "No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias" (Maier et al. 2022) is itself strong prima facie evidence that when a leading team applied standard bias-correction methods to the Mertens et al. dataset, the corrected effect was not distinguishable from zero — that is a fact this report was unable to independently quote/verify, but its existence and title (confirmed via citation) point toward H2/a near-null corrected result rather than genuine unanswerability. If one credits the plain meaning of that title over the methodological critique of PET-PEESE's unreliability under heterogeneity, the more assertive conclusion is that bias-corrected nudge effects are close to zero, which would argue against nudges as a broadly effective policy tool. This report treats that as unconfirmed only because the primary Maier et al. quote/numbers were not fetched and audited — a genuine researcher with more budget might reasonably weight the title alone as sufficient signal to lean toward H2.
whatWouldChangeThisCall: Directly fetching and auditing Maier et al. (2022)'s reported bias-corrected effect size (with CI) and comparing it numerically to Mertens et al.'s raw pooled Cohen's d - this is the single missing hinge number.

Finding a peer-reviewed source applying multiple independent bias-correction methods (p-curve, PET-PEESE, trim-and-fill, selection models) to the same nudge dataset and reporting whether they converge - would resolve H4 in favor of H1 or H2.
Locating large pre-registered government/nudge-unit trial data (e.g., DellaVigna & Linos's 126 RCTs) with a directly reported average effect size comparable to the corrected academic estimate.
Verifying nudge-category-specific bias-corrected effect sizes (defaults vs. social norms vs. reminders) from a source that survives adversarial audit, to test H3.
Any cost-effectiveness analysis of nudges versus alternative policy tools post-correction, which was never gathered and is necessary to complete the practical policy-relevance half of the question.
baseRate: No outside-view base rate for 'fraction of published behavioral-economics/psychology effects that survive rigorous publication-bias correction' was present in the confirmed evidence. Its absence is notable: prior general literature (e.g., psychology replication crisis findings) commonly cites base rates like ~50% of significant published effects failing to replicate or shrinking substantially under bias correction, but no such general base rate appears in the audited claims here, so none is asserted as fact in this report.

findings.claim: Mertens et al. (2022, PNAS) meta-analysis found nudging effective across a large pooled sample (455 effect sizes, 214 publications, N=2,149,683), using Cohen's d as the effect measure and excluding studies that combined choice architecture with other interventions to isolate the pure nudge effect.
findings.evidence: Verbatim-matched quotes on sample composition (455 effect sizes/214 publications/N=2,149,683), Cohen's d as effect measure, and exclusion criteria; audit supported on all three.

findings.claim: Maier et al. (2022, PNAS) published a direct rebuttal, 'No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias,' explicitly re-analyzing the same/related literature using bias-correction methods and reaching the opposite headline conclusion from Mertens et al.
findings.evidence: Bibliographic citation confirms title, authorship, journal, year, and DOI; the claim is corroborated by a secondary source (a Nature Human Behaviour piece) rather than by fetching the Maier paper itself.
findings.citationCheck: partial - the cited page is a third-party manifesto article, not the Maier et al. paper; it confirms the paper's existence/title/venue via its own reference list but was not used to verify Maier's actual corrected effect-size results or methodology in detail.

findings.claim: The core statistical method used to 'correct' for publication bias in this literature (FAT-PET-PEESE / PET-PEESE) is unreliable for testing bias and for hypothesis-testing the true effect - and less efficient at estimating the mean effect - precisely under heterogeneity (differing population effects across and within studies), which is the realistic condition for a literature as varied as nudge research. It performs especially poorly with few studies, small samples, and high heterogeneity.
findings.evidence: Two independent peer-reviewed methodological sources converge: jrsm.1298 shows FPP only performs well under an unrealistic fixed-effects assumption and becomes unreliable under heterogeneity (for bias-testing and hypothesis-testing), and is less efficient for mean-effect estimation; a separate 2017 source states PET-PEESE performs poorly with few studies, small samples, and high heterogeneity - conditions plausibly present in nudge meta-analyses.
findings.citationCheck: supported on both; the connection of these general statistical findings specifically to the nudge literature's own heterogeneity profile is this report's inference, not a directly audited claim.

findings.claim: There is a genuine, documented methodological contradiction in the literature about how well PET-PEESE-type corrections work: one source (jrsm.1298) says FPP 'becomes unreliable' under heterogeneity, while a related Stanley/Doucouliagos-lineage source claims PET-PEESE has properties 'much better than conventional meta-analysis' even under adverse conditions.
findings.evidence: Explicitly flagged as a contradiction during gap analysis; both sources are peer-reviewed methods papers, but they disagree on how much confidence to place in PET-PEESE-family corrections under realistic (heterogeneous, small-sample) conditions.
findings.citationCheck: supported - both underlying claims individually passed audit; the contradiction between them is a synthesis-level observation, not itself audited as a single claim.

findings.claim: There is broader academic acknowledgment (independent of the Mertens/Maier dispute) that empirical effectiveness of nudge-type interventions is mixed across domains: digital nudging studies show inconsistent effects on user behavior, and a 2023 policy-administration piece notes 'growing concern' about the efficacy of some nudge interventions despite nudging's continued policy popularity.
findings.evidence: PLOS ONE systematic review states digital nudging effectiveness is 'not fully conclusive' with mixed study results; Public Administration Review 2023 paper states nudging faces 'growing concern' about efficacy of some interventions and proposes a 4S framework (sufficient, scalable, subjective, statistically significant) beyond mere significance.
findings.citationCheck: supported on both; note these are domain-general/qualitative statements, not quantitative bias-correction results.

findings.claim: In the one domain with detailed quantitative evidence captured (COVID-19 vaccination nudges), effects are real but small: a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs (167,127 individuals) found a significant but modest pooled effect (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.07-1.33, p<0.01), and a separate large-scale study (two RCTs totaling N=336,854, plus a 124-RCT/20M-participant dataset) concluded nudges promote vaccination only 'with small magnitude' and require combination with other strategies to meaningfully move behavior.
findings.evidence: Both sources are primary but of unconfirmed/lower tier (T?, includes a preprint and an SSRN working paper, not peer-reviewed journal publications); numbers directly quoted and audit-supported, but this is a single applied domain (vaccination), not a publication-bias-corrected estimate of the general nudge literature.
findings.citationCheck: supported on the quoted numbers; caution: T? tier (preprint/working paper) means this is not yet peer-reviewed, and it does not itself represent a publication-bias correction of the broader literature - it is a domain-specific raw/pooled effect.

caveats: The confirmed evidence set never captured the single most decisive fact needed to answer the question directly: Maier et al.'s actual bias-corrected effect-size number(s) versus Mertens et al.'s raw pooled effect size, or a p-curve/PEESE-corrected estimate with a confidence interval showing whether it crosses zero. The coverage checklist explicitly lists this as unanswered ("By what magnitude do bias-corrected effect sizes shrink... and do corrected estimates remain distinguishable from zero?" - unanswered). Several supporting claims are T? tier (unconfirmed source tier, including a preprint and an SSRN working paper) rather than T1/T2 peer-reviewed journal sources, and one key claim (Maier et al.'s paper details) was audited only via a third-party citation, not the primary source itself (partial). 16 lower-ranked claims were never verified due to research budget limits and are excluded here. Several claims were explicitly refuted/killed during adversarial review, including a claimed Science study on court-appearance nudges, a claimed COVID-vaccine-nudge time-decay finding, a claimed successful "dark room" dishonesty replication, a claimed pro-nudge conclusion from the 2016 Vlaev et al. review, a claimed DellaVigna-Linos linkage, a claimed nudge-category subgroup breakdown, and a claimed DellaVigna & Linos NBER working paper citation - none of these can be used as evidence in either direction. Nudge-type heterogeneity (H3) and cost-effectiveness comparisons were never evidenced in the confirmed set. The topic is time-sensitive: the Mertens (2022) vs. Maier (2022) dispute is recent and actively contested, and methodological consensus on PET-PEESE-family corrections is itself unsettled (see contradiction below), so any verdict here should be treated as provisional pending resolution of that methods debate.

honestLimits.falseKillRateUnmeasured: This report kills claims. How often it kills a TRUE one has never been measured — here or anywhere in the published literature. Read `refuted` before concluding something is unsupported.
honestLimits.reliabilityNotValidity: `calibration` measures whether the panel repeats itself, not whether it is right. An LLM panel has been recorded agreeing with itself at alpha 0.77 while being systematically wrong. A high kappa never licenses 'the panel is correct'.
honestLimits.confirmedMeans: `confirmed` means 'survived a filter of unknown accuracy', not 'true'.

honestLimits.quotesAreLocatedInCode: Every claim's verbatim quote is searched for in the exact page text the extractor was shown, in code, before the panel votes - see `quoteAudit` and `stats.quoteLocation`. A quote the engine could not fully locate was assembled from more than one place or had wording added, and is a defect in the EVIDENCE regardless of whether the claim is true. `unverifiable` means the page was empty or the quote too short to judge, and is never evidence of fabrication. Measured over 30 real quotes on 2026-09-08: 93% located.
honestLimits.partialCitationsAreKept: A `partial` citation verdict means the page points this way but the statement adds scope, certainty or specificity the page does not carry - and it does NOT remove the claim. Only `unsupported` does. Measured with injected defects: an inflated number, an invented attribution and an inflated scope all came back `partial`, so all three would have been published. Read `citationPartials` before quoting a number or an attribution from this report.
honestLimits.framingProvenance: scopeContract.provenance says, per field, whether the asker SUPPLIED it or the model DRAFTED it. A drafted assumption and a supplied one look identical in the JSON and mean opposite things: a supplied field is a decision to respect, a drafted one is a premise the run should have tested.
honestLimits.irrelevantSearchResults: stats.pickStarvation counts how often the source picker was handed search hits and chose NONE of them. A high rate means search returned results that were not about the question - a poisoned or rate-limited upstream engine - and NOT that the web is silent. searchHealth counts results, not relevance, so it reads as healthy in exactly this case.
honestLimits.archivedCopies: A source whose `via` is `wayback` was read from the Internet Archive, not live: the publisher blocked the fetch. `snapshotDate` says when the copy was captured, and it matters - the provenance lens judges recency, and an archived page is as old as its snapshot, not as old as today. The archive is used ONLY after a live read failed or returned an abstract-only stub.
honestLimits.abstractOnlySources: stats.fetchVia counts how each source was READ. `crossref-fallback` means the publisher blocked the fetch and only the abstract was available, and those sources carry `abstractOnly: true`. A claim verified against an abstract has been checked against a summary of the paper, not the paper.
honestLimits.searchCoverage: Check stats.searchHealth. If every general-web backend reports 0 results, this run saw a scholarly-only slice of the web and its coverage gaps are a search artefact rather than evidence that nothing exists.
